passages.t: A Levite, his concubine, and a father who would not let them go
passages.happening:
“Now in those days, when there was no king in Israel, a Levite who lived in the remote hill country of Ephraim took for himself a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah” (verse 1).

She leaves him and goes back to her father's house in Bethlehem. After four months the Levite goes after her, ‘to speak kindly to her and bring her back’, with his servant and two donkeys. Her father welcomes him gladly (verses 2-3).

The father keeps him for three days of eating and drinking (verse 4). On the fourth day the Levite rises early to leave, but the father urges him to eat first, and then to stay another night (verses 5-7). On the fifth day it happens again, and they eat together until late afternoon (verse 8). When the Levite at last gets up to go, the father begs him once more to stay, since the day is nearly over (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
The second of the book's closing stories begins with the same words as the first: there was no king in Israel.

A concubine was a secondary wife. She was bound to a man by law, but without the full place of a first wife, and often she came from a poorer family. The story never gives her name, and she never speaks a word. The Hebrew word for concubine comes eight times in the chapter, always in place of a name.

Why she left is not clear. The Hebrew text says she was unfaithful to him. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, and some readers take it that she became angry with him, which may fit better with her going home to her father. Either way, the Levite goes after her to ‘speak kindly to her’, word for word to speak to her heart, a phrase used elsewhere for comfort and reconciliation. Hold on to that phrase. The rest of the story shows how far he fell from it.

Hospitality was a sacred duty in that world, and the father's repeated urging to stay shows it, perhaps pressed to excess. The scene is slow and repetitive, almost comic: one more meal, one more night. But it has a purpose. It makes them leave late, and the late start leads to disaster.

Bethlehem appears here in a kindly light, a place of welcome. Bethlehem was the home of the Levite in chapter 17 too, and it will be the home of Ruth's family and of King David.
passages.later:
The same idiom, to speak to the heart, is used by God himself when he promises to win back his unfaithful people: “I will allure her and lead her to the wilderness, and speak to her tenderly” (Hosea 2:14).

The book of Ruth, set in the same days of the judges, begins with a family from Bethlehem in Judah (Ruth 1:1).
passages.asks: The Levite set out to speak to a woman's heart. Ask whether the people closest to you would say you speak to their hearts, or only about what you want from them. And notice how the story slows down over a few meals. Ask what small delays and comforts in your life have quietly shaped where you end up.

passages.t: No room in Gibeah, except with an old man
passages.happening:
Late in the day the Levite leaves at last, with his concubine, his servant and his donkeys. Near Jebus, which is Jerusalem, the servant asks to stop there for the night (verses 10-11). His master refuses. “We will not turn aside to the city of foreigners, where there are no Israelites. We will go on to Gibeah” (verse 12).

The sun sets as they reach Gibeah, a town of Benjamin. They sit down in the town square, ‘but no one would take them into his home for the night’ (verse 15).

That evening an old man comes in from his work in the fields. He is from the hill country of Ephraim, living in Gibeah as an outsider (verse 16). He asks where they are going. The Levite tells him and says they have everything they need, only no one has taken them in (verses 17-19). “Peace to you,” said the old man. “Let me supply everything you need. Only do not spend the night in the square” (verse 20). He takes them home, feeds the donkeys, and they wash their feet and eat and drink (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Jebus was still held by the Jebusites. Israel would not take it until David's day. The Levite refuses to stay among foreigners. He chooses an Israelite town for safety. The story is about to show that he found no safety there.

Gibeah lay a few miles north of Jerusalem, in the land of Benjamin. Its exact site is debated. It later became the hometown of Saul, Israel's first king.

In that world, travelers depended on hospitality, and a town that left strangers in its square at night was failing a sacred duty. No one in Gibeah opens a door. The only one who does is himself an outsider, a man from Ephraim.

The old man's welcome is warm: ‘Peace to you’. Washing the feet and sharing food were the signs of a guest received. For a moment the story seems to have found its safe place.
passages.later:
The story of Sodom begins the same way, with visitors taken in for the night by a man who was himself a newcomer in the town, and then: “Before they had gone to bed, all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house” (Genesis 19:4).

Saul's home was this same town: “Saul also went to his home in Gibeah” (1 Samuel 10:26).
passages.asks: The Levite avoided a foreign city to be safe among his own people, and his own people were the danger. Ask where you assume you are safe simply because you are among people like you. And think of the old man, an outsider, who was the only one to open his door. Ask whose door is open in your town to the stranger in the square, and whether it is yours.

passages.happening:
While they are eating, the wicked men of the town surround the house and pound on the door. They demand that the old man bring out his guest so that they can have relations with him (verse 22).

The old man goes out to them. He calls what they want a wicked thing and an outrage. Then he offers them his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine instead (verses 23-24).

The men will not listen. “So the Levite took his concubine and sent her outside to them, and they raped her and abused her throughout the night, and at dawn they let her go” (verse 25).

At daybreak she comes back to the house where her master is staying, falls at the door, and lies there until it is light (verse 26). In the morning, when he opens the door to leave, there she is, collapsed in the doorway, ‘with her hands on the threshold’ (verse 27). He tells her to get up and go. There is no answer (verse 28). He puts her on his donkey and goes home.

At home he takes a knife, cuts her body into twelve pieces, and sends them through all the territory of Israel (verse 29). Everyone who sees it says, “Nothing like this has been seen or done from the day the Israelites came out of the land of Egypt until this day. Think it over, take counsel, and speak up!” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
These verses describe rape, murder and the cutting up of a woman's body. They are told plainly in the text, and these notes tell them plainly and do not linger.

The likeness to the story of Sodom in Genesis 19 is deliberate. A visitor is taken in by a man who is himself a stranger in the town. The men of the town surround the house and demand the guest. The host offers women in his place. In Genesis the angels rescue those inside. Here no one does. An Israelite town has become like Sodom.

The old man's offer reflects a world in which protecting a male guest was ranked above the safety of women. The story does not accept that ranking. It exposes it in all its horror.

Then the Levite, the man who set out to speak to her heart, pushes her out of the door to save himself. In the morning he opens the door to go on his way, finds her there, and tells her to get up. The Hebrew never says when she died. When he speaks to her, there is simply no answer. The image of her hands on the threshold, the doorway that should have been safety, is one of the most painful in Scripture.

Cutting up an animal and sending the pieces through the tribes was a summons to war. Saul will later do it with oxen. The Levite does it with a woman.

The nation's answer is shock: nothing like this had happened since Israel came out of Egypt. Its last words are a call: think it over, take counsel, and speak up. The text does not ask anyone to stay silent about such a wrong.
passages.later:
Hosea, centuries later, remembered this as a byword for the depth of Israel's corruption: “They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah” (Hosea 9:9).

The notes on Genesis 19 call Lot's offer of his daughters wrong and say that the text does not praise it. The same is true here.

Scripture calls God's people to do the opposite of what Gibeah did: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed” (Proverbs 31:8).
passages.hard:
Why is such a story in the Bible, and why does the text seem to say so little to condemn it?

The story is in Scripture because it is true to what people, God's people included, can become. And it serves the book's purpose. Judges is showing what happens when Israel leaves the LORD and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The narrator presents these days as the depths of Israel's lawlessness, and never as a pattern. He condemns by the way he tells it: the likeness to Sodom, the woman's silence, her hands on the threshold, and the Levite's heartless words. In the next chapter the Levite gives his own account to the tribes, and it leaves out what he did. There is no word from God anywhere in this chapter. That too is the point. This is Israel without God's rule.

Many readers have drawn attention to how the text exposes violence against women by keeping the reader's eyes on her suffering. The scholar Phyllis Trible did so in her book Texts of Terror (1984).

Any reading that excuses these men or blames the woman is a misreading, and it must be rejected. Whatever had happened between her and the Levite before, nothing in it makes her responsible for what was done to her. The men of Gibeah, the old man who offered her, and the Levite who pushed her out each answer for what they did, and the text gives none of them a word of defense. The site's page on abuse and its cover-up sets out why harm done among the people of God must be brought into the light and reported, never hidden.

A word for anyone who has been sexually assaulted. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. Where you were, what you wore, whether you fought back: none of it makes it your fault. Please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The story never gives the woman a name or a word. Ask whom you have overlooked in the same way, the people whose suffering is in the room but never spoken of. Then hear the nation's call, ‘Think it over, take counsel, and speak up’. Ask what wrong among people you know you have kept quiet about, and whom you should tell.
